subtype: Approach: falling in love with the idea [Pitfall]
passage: Yamini, you asked what I would do differently, so let me be honest, from Ankita's side. I told everyone about my idea, a subscription box of snacks for students. Friends said, "Wow, so good!" A cousin said, "Hmm, maybe check the price?" and I nodded and moved on. I was in love. Within a month I had paid a designer for a logo, bought a domain, built a website with a tiny payment button. Then I asked people I did not know, at the bus stop, in the library. Not one wanted the box. Three said "cute". My savings were gone, and I had nothing to show but a nicely designed page. I should have asked strangers before anything else.

qa.q: What kind of business was Ankita's idea?
qa.a: It was a subscription box of snacks for students.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling in the early weeks after telling friends about the idea?
qa.a: Ankita was in love with the idea, excited and sure, which is why the cousin's polite doubt was brushed aside.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Ankita have used first, and why?
qa.a: Ankita could have asked strangers whether they would pay for a small trial box, because friends tend to be kind while strangers show real interest.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt when the doubt was ignored?
qa.a: The cousin probably felt unheard, since the polite question about the price got only a nod.

grounding: Shows falling in love with an idea: hearing mostly praise, brushing aside doubts, spending savings on branding before testing demand with strangers.

subtype: Approach: falling in love with the idea [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Kishore, Hansa's classmate, and I watched the whole thing happen in the college canteen. Hansa had an idea: a monthly box of healthy snacks for hostel students. Every friend at our table said, "Wow, I'd totally buy it." Nobody asked what it would cost. When Priya said, gently, "Would people pay every month, though? Most of us live on instant noodles," Hansa laughed it off. "They'll pay for good stuff." Within three weeks Hansa had spent her savings on a logo, a website with a rotating banner, and printed stickers. In the first week after launch, the website had forty visitors and two orders, both from us. I don't know what Hansa was thinking then. She seemed so sure. But I remember Priya's question going unanswered, and I still think about it.

qa.q: How many orders came in the first week?
How did Hansa seem to feel about the idea?
qa.a: Hansa seemed very sure and excited, laughing off Priya's gentle doubt.

qa.q: What would you change first before spending on a logo?
qa.a: Ask strangers, not just friends, whether they would pay every month, perhaps with a small paid trial, before spending on branding.

qa.q: How might Priya feel about the question being laughed off?
qa.a: Priya may feel brushed aside, and sad to see that polite doubt proven right after the savings were spent.

grounding: Shows a founder hearing only friends' praise, brushing off a polite doubt, and spending savings on a logo and website before checking whether strangers want the product.

subtype: Approach: falling in love with the idea [Pitfall]
passage:
September. Uday's idea arrived at 2 am: a campus app for renting out textbooks from seniors to juniors. At breakfast, four friends called it genius. Devika asked quietly, "Do juniors actually want old books, or do they just photocopy?" Uday waved it away. "Everyone needs books."
October. Uday spent most of his summer internship savings on a designer's logo and a polished website with a bookshelf animation. He didn't message a single junior outside his friend group.
November. Launch week. He posted in every college group. Eighty-three visits, zero rentals. One junior replied: "We just photocopy the important chapters, bhaiya." Uday read it three times. Then he opened his notes and found Devika's question from September, which he had typed out and never answered.

qa.a: A campus app for renting out textbooks from seniors to juniors.

qa.q: How did Uday feel reading the junior's reply?
qa.a: Uday was stunned and deflated, reading it three times as he realised Devika's early doubt had been right.

qa.q: What else could Uday have done in September?
qa.a: Uday could have asked a few juniors outside the friend group whether they'd rent books, or rented a handful by hand, before spending.

qa.q: How might Devika see the launch week?
qa.a: Devika may feel sorry for Uday but also unheard, since her September question pointed at exactly this problem.

grounding: Illustrates a founder who listens only to encouraging friends, ignores a quiet doubt, and spends savings on branding before testing with strangers.
